subject: Chemistry
title: Element 118: The End of the Table?
description: One-minute skill: Element 118: The End of the Table?.

hook.text: The periodic table currently ends at element 118. Scientists are already trying to make 119 and 120.

buildup.text: Every element past uranium (92) was created artificially. The heavier they get, the harder they are to make.

discovery.text: Element 118 took thousands of hours of bombardment to produce just three atoms.

twist.text: Elements 119 and 120 would start a new row. But current accelerators may not be powerful enough.

climax.text: Japan, Russia, and Germany are racing to be first. The periodic table is still being written.

punchline.text: Row 8 hasn't started yet. The table has no last page.

quiz.question: Why is it so hard to create elements beyond 118?
options: Current particle accelerators may not be powerful enough
Scientists have lost interest in heavy elements
There are no target materials left to use

details.summary: Oganesson, element 118, was first synthesized in 2002 at Russia's Joint Institute for Nuclear Research by bombarding californium-249 with calcium-48 ions. Named after physicist Yuri Oganessian, it is the heaviest element confirmed to date and completes the seventh period of the periodic table.
details.whyItMatters: Oganesson marks the current frontier of element creation. Its predicted properties are wildly different from other noble gases, suggesting relativistic effects may fundamentally alter chemistry for the heaviest elements.
takeaways: Oganesson (element 118) is the heaviest confirmed element on the periodic table
Only five or six atoms have ever been produced, each lasting milliseconds
Theoretical predictions suggest it may behave nothing like other noble gases

faq.question: Why might oganesson behave differently from other noble gases?
faq.answer: At atomic number 118, electrons move at significant fractions of light speed, causing relativistic effects that alter orbital shapes and energies..

faq.question: Can we ever know oganesson's true chemical properties?
faq.answer: With only millisecond lifetimes and single-atom production, direct chemical experimentation is currently impossible. Properties are inferred from theoretical calculations using relativistic quantum mechanics..
